subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 spoken-English task on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Plan and structure a presentation (introduction, signposting, conclusion)
Use Standard English and choose the right formal or informal register
Deliver effectively using pace, pause, emphasis, eye contact and body language
Take part in discussion and debate: make a point, give reasons and evidence, build on and challenge others
Listen actively and respond to others
Adapt tone and register for audience and purpose

questions.lo: Plan and structure a presentation (introduction, signposting, conclusion)
questions.q: What are the three main parts of a well-structured presentation, in order?
options: Conclusion, introduction, main points
Introduction, main points, conclusion
Main points, conclusion, introduction
Introduction, conclusion, main points
questions.explain: A clear talk opens with an introduction (a hook and what's coming), develops the main points, then finishes with a conclusion that sums up. This order lets the audience follow you the first (and only) time they hear it.

questions.lo: Plan and structure a presentation (introduction, signposting, conclusion)
questions.q: What does 'signposting' mean in a spoken presentation?
options: Using slides with lots of pictures
Signalling your structure out loud with phrases like 'Firstly...' and 'To sum up...'
Standing next to a sign so people can see you
Writing your whole speech on cards
questions.explain: Signposting means telling listeners where you are going and where you have been, using phrases such as 'Firstly', 'My next point is' and 'To sum up'. Because an audience can't re-read your talk, signposting keeps them on track.

questions.lo: Plan and structure a presentation (introduction, signposting, conclusion)
questions.q: You are opening a persuasive talk about school lunches. Which opening is most effective?
options: "Sorry, I didn't really prepare, so bear with me."
"School lunches. Um. There's stuff to say I guess."
"Every lunchtime, food we could enjoy ends up in the bin. Today I'll give you three ways to make school lunches better."
"You all know about lunches already, so I'll skip the start."
questions.explain: The best opening grabs attention with a hook and then signposts what's coming ('three ways'). Apologising or diving in with no shape weakens the talk before it begins.

questions.lo: Use Standard English and choose the right formal or informal register
questions.q: Which statement about Standard English is TRUE?
options: It is a posh accent that only some people can use
It is the widely-understood form of English with agreed grammar and vocabulary, and can be spoken in any accent
It means never using any full sentences
It is only used when writing, never when speaking
questions.explain: Standard English is about grammar and word choice, not accent. A speaker with any regional accent can use perfect Standard English, and it is used in both formal writing and formal speech.

questions.lo: Use Standard English and choose the right formal or informal register
questions.q: In a formal debate, which sentence uses Standard English?
options: "We should not have changed the timetable."
"We shouldn't of changed the timetable."
"We didn't done nothing to the timetable."
"We ain't got no problem with the timetable."
questions.explain: Standard English avoids non-standard forms like 'shouldn't of', double negatives ('ain't got no') and errors like 'didn't done'. 'We should not have' is the correct standard form.

questions.lo: Use Standard English and choose the right formal or informal register
questions.q: Which sentence is written in a FORMAL register?
options: "Hiya, you good? Wanna hang out later?"
"Dunno, it's well boring though."
"I would like to request a meeting to discuss this issue."
"Nah, can't be bothered with that."
questions.explain: A formal register avoids slang and contractions and chooses precise vocabulary. 'I would like to request a meeting' is formal; the others are informal, using slang like 'wanna', 'dunno' and 'nah'.

questions.lo: Use Standard English and choose the right formal or informal register
questions.q: What does 'register' mean when we talk about spoken English?
options: The list of who is present in the room
How loud your voice is
How formal or informal your language is, chosen to fit your audience and purpose
The order you plan your points in
questions.explain: Register is the level of formality in your language. You slide between formal and informal depending on who you are speaking to and why.

questions.lo: Deliver effectively using pace, pause, emphasis, eye contact and body language
questions.q: Why is a short PAUSE before a key point a useful delivery technique?
options: It lets you check your phone
It builds suspense and makes the audience focus on what comes next
It shows you have forgotten your speech
It makes the talk finish faster
questions.explain: A deliberate pause creates suspense and draws the audience's attention to the important point that follows. Well-timed silence is a powerful delivery tool.

questions.lo: Deliver effectively using pace, pause, emphasis, eye contact and body language
questions.q: A nervous speaker keeps reading straight from their notes and never looks up. Which delivery skill should they work on most?
options: Eye contact with the audience
Using longer words
Talking as fast as possible
Standing further away
questions.explain: Looking at the audience instead of the notes or floor is eye contact. It connects the speaker with listeners and makes delivery far more engaging and confident.

questions.lo: Deliver effectively using pace, pause, emphasis, eye contact and body language
questions.q: A speaker rushes through their whole talk so fast the audience can't keep up. Which aspect of delivery needs fixing?
options: Their vocabulary
Their pace
Their eye contact
Their conclusion
questions.explain: Pace is the speed of speaking. Slowing down slightly sounds more confident and makes a talk far easier to follow.

questions.lo: Take part in discussion and debate: make a point, give reasons and evidence, build on and challenge others
questions.q: A strong contribution in a debate usually contains which three elements?
options: A joke, an insult and a shout
A point, a reason and evidence or an example
A question, a pause and a slide
An apology, an opinion and a guess
questions.explain: The clearest debate contributions state a point, give a reason ('because...'), and back it up with evidence or an example. Opinion on its own is far less convincing.

questions.lo: Take part in discussion and debate: make a point, give reasons and evidence, build on and challenge others
questions.q: Another student argues that phones should be banned in school. You disagree. Which is the best POLITE challenge?
options: "That's a ridiculous thing to say."
"You're wrong, next point."
"I see why you'd say that, but I disagree, because phones can be useful learning tools, and here's an example..."
Talk over them until they stop.
questions.explain: A polite, effective challenge acknowledges the other speaker, disagrees respectfully, and gives a reason. Insults, dismissals and interrupting all shut down a structured discussion.

questions.lo: Take part in discussion and debate: make a point, give reasons and evidence, build on and challenge others
questions.q: Sam says the school day should start later. You agree and want to add to their idea. Which phrase best BUILDS ON their point?
options: "Building on Sam's point, I'd add that teenagers concentrate better later in the morning."
"Anyway, changing the subject completely..."
"That's obvious, everyone knows that."
"I wasn't really listening, but okay."
questions.explain: Building on means adding to what someone else said, linking to it clearly ('Building on Sam's point...'). This keeps the discussion connected and shows you listened.

questions.lo: Listen actively and respond to others
questions.q: Which of these is a sign of ACTIVE listening in a discussion?
options: Planning your own point while the other person is still talking
Summarising what they said ('So you're saying...') before you respond
Interrupting to speak sooner
Looking at your phone while they talk
questions.explain: Active listening means focusing on the speaker and showing you understood, for example by summarising their point before responding. Interrupting or being distracted are the opposite.

questions.lo: Listen actively and respond to others
questions.q: Why is listening described as 'part of speaking well' in a structured discussion?
options: Because the person who talks most always wins
Because you can't build on or challenge an idea properly if you didn't really hear it
Because listening means you never have to speak
Because it lets you copy the teacher exactly
questions.explain: The strongest contributors summarise and build on others, which is only possible if they listened carefully first. Talking the most is not the same as speaking effectively.

questions.lo: Adapt tone and register for audience and purpose
questions.q: You want to suggest a new lunchtime club. Which version best suits a FORMAL email to the head teacher?
options: "Yo, we should totally start a games club, it'd be class."
"I would like to propose a new lunchtime club, as I believe it would benefit students."
"Games club. Do it. Trust me."
"Dunno if you'd be up for it but a club would be cool."
questions.explain: Adapting tone and register to your audience means choosing a formal, polite version for the head teacher. The message is the same, but the register shifts to fit who is listening and why.

questions.lo: Adapt tone and register for audience and purpose
questions.q: Which situation calls for the MOST formal tone and register?
options: Chatting with your best friend at break
Sending a quick message in a group chat
Speaking in a formal school debate
Telling a joke to your football team
questions.explain: A formal debate needs a fairly formal register: precise vocabulary, Standard English and few contractions. Chats with friends can be informal, because the audience and purpose are different.

questions.lo: Deliver effectively using pace, pause, emphasis, eye contact and body language
questions.q: Why does rehearsing a speech or a performance of a poem improve delivery?
options: It guarantees you will never feel nervous
It makes delivery smoother and more confident, so pace, pauses and expression work better
It removes the need for any structure
It means you can read every word off the page
questions.explain: Rehearsal makes delivery smooth and controlled, letting you use pace, pause, emphasis and expression deliberately for effect rather than stumbling or reading flatly.

questions.lo: Use Standard English and choose the right formal or informal register
questions.q: Rewrite for a formal debate: "We ain't got no reason to change it, it's well good." Which is the best Standard-English version?
options: "We haven't got no reason to change it, it's well good."
"There is no strong reason to change it, as it works well."
"We ain't changing nothing, it's good yeah."
"We got no reasons and it's well good, innit."
questions.explain: The Standard-English fix removes the double negative ('ain't got no') and the slang ('well good'), replacing them with correct grammar and precise vocabulary suitable for a formal register.
